set.population: Adults who use classic psychedelics: people who planned a psychedelic experience on their own initiative and signed up online (one prospective study), healthy volunteers given LSD in laboratory studies, and people recalling past experiences in surveys
set.magnitude: Haijen et al. (2018), standardized coefficients adjusted for one another and for self-estimated amount (about 198 people): set and challenging experience −0.32 (SE 0.07); recreational or social intentions −0.22 (SE 0.08); clear intentions and mystical-type 0.18, visual 0.16, challenging −0.13 (p = 0.088); absorption and challenging 0.22, mystical-type 0.35; R2 0.32 for challenging experience. Vizeli et al. (2024): directions and significance only (sizes are in a figure and a supplement not used): pre-dose well-being with stronger effects on all self-rated scales but three, the anxiety scales included; pre-dose anxiety with more anxiety during the session. Recalled afterwards: surrender r = 0.72 with mystical-type experience, preoccupation 0.64 and confusion 0.58 with dread (n = 143, one of the two retrospective studies, as summarized by Aday et al., 2021); negative mindset blamed for the most challenging experience: beta 0.14, harm thoughts or attempts OR 4.56 (95% CI 2.10 to 9.94), adjusted only for the other attributions (Simonsson et al., 2023).
set.plain: People who felt calm, open and ready the day before a trip they had planned rated it as less difficult. In laboratory LSD sessions, feeling anxious beforehand went with more anxiety, while feeling well went with stronger effects overall, not easier ones. These links come from watching, not testing, and many people dropped out of the study outside the laboratory. Studies in which people recalled their mood afterwards found bigger links, but memories can be coloured by how the trip went.
set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: The prospective study is at high risk of bias (drug type, psychiatric history and other drugs not adjusted; the amount estimated after the experience; about 70% of the baseline sample not in the analysis; when the day-before survey was completed could not be confirmed, and it could be filled in on paper and entered later), the laboratory analysis has some concerns (each predictor adjusted for dose only; no sizes in the text), and the recalled-state findings are at very high risk (attributions made at the same sitting as the outcome) and are worded only as associations (cards sc_haijen_2018, sc_vizeli_2024, sc_aday_2021, sc_simonsson_2023).
set.grade.domains.inconsistency.note: More anxiety, alone or within a worse overall state of mind, measured before the drug went with a more anxious or more challenging experience in both the naturalistic and the laboratory source. In the laboratory a better general mood went with stronger effects overall, the anxiety scales included by the text, rather than with a less challenging session; that is a different mood scale and outcome from the naturalistic study's set component, so the claim states it instead of rating it as inconsistency (the certainty would stay very low either way). Absorption's link with mystical and challenging experience alike is reported, not a conflict.
set.grade.reasoning: Predictor studies start low, even inside randomized laboratory studies, because the predictors were not randomized; down one for risk of bias, giving very low. Status replicated, for the direction only: more anxiety beforehand, alone or within a worse overall state of mind, went with a more anxious or more challenging experience in two independent sources measured before the drug, one prospective and naturalistic (Imperial College London, the set component) and one laboratory (Basel, pre-dose anxiety), with different questionnaires, so it is a conceptual replication; recalled attributions in an independent panel (Simonsson et al.) point the same way. That a better mood goes with an easier experience rests on the naturalistic study alone: in the laboratory a better mood went with stronger effects overall. The other predictors rest on single studies or on states recalled afterwards. The review (Aday et al., 2021) is used only for what it adds (the retrospective Russ studies and the tabulation of absorption), since its Table 1 misprints the sign for set.

evidence_set: No statistically significant association (p < 0.05) with any of the acute measures: openness, emotional stability, trait anxiety, suggestibility, stubbornness, number of lifetime uses, self-rated experience, and a retreat or therapeutically designed setting.

Openness predicted 5D-ASC oceanic boundlessness, spiritual experience and insightfulness and the MEQ30 total, mystical and positive-mood scores; neuroticism, agreeableness and conscientiousness showed no significant association with any LSD effect.

All state predictors in the review's abstract (surrender, apprehension, preoccupation, confusion) come from two studies marked retrospective, Russ 2019a (n = 183) and Russ 2019b (n = 143), both of people who had used psilocybin; in Russ 2019b surrender correlated r = 0.72 with mystical-type experience, and preoccupation r = 0.64 and confusion r = 0.58 with dread.

set.plain: In surveys, people who felt safe and supported during a trip reported a little less fear and fewer difficulties, but they rated both afterwards. The only study among these that asked people beforehand found only a weak, uncertain link between feeling good about the place and the people and how the trip went, and no detectable difference for retreats or settings designed for therapy. No study put people in different settings on purpose to compare them.
set.grade.domains.inconsistency.note: The direction differs by aspect: support and safety went with fewer difficulties in two retrospective surveys, but blaming the people around showed no association with challenge (and, if anything, lower odds of harm thoughts) in the panel survey; in the prospective study the setting rating showed only a non-significant trend in the same direction, and a retreat or therapeutic setting no association.
set.grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down two for risk of bias and one for inconsistency, giving very low (the floor). Status mixed: four independent studies; support and safety went with fewer difficulties in two retrospective surveys (Perkins et al.; the no-support attribution in Simonsson et al.) and the untested party comparison points the same way, but blaming the people around showed no such link, and the one prospective study found only a non-significant trend for its setting rating (and a weak link with well-being two weeks later) and no association for a retreat or therapeutic setting; recall at the same sitting may explain part of the difference, but no study has shown that it does.

set.plain: In one large survey, people who felt safe and supported at their last ayahuasca ceremony recalled a little less fear and fewer problems in the weeks after. Being offered a chance to talk things through beforehand went with fewer problems afterwards, but not with less fear, and fasting showed no detectable link with either. The same people rated the ceremony and their experience, looking back, and the differences were small.
